answers.primary: A dynamic workflow. Claude writes a JavaScript orchestration script that lists the route handler files, runs one audit agent per file with pipeline(), and then runs a second adversarial verification phase over each finding before it is reported. Save that run's script from /workflows with `s` into .claude/workflows/ so next quarter it reruns as a single /command, passing the target paths through the `args` global.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents fanned out from the conversation turn by turn. At 400 files Claude has to re-decide each batch, every agent result lands in the main context window, and the only repeatable artifact is the worker definition rather than the orchestration itself.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the saved script, so the per-file fan-out and the adversarial verification phase are code the runtime runs, not judgment Claude re-exercises each quarter. The model still owns what any individual audit agent concludes inside a phase.
answers.context_boundary: The script runs in an isolated workflow runtime, separate from your conversation, and intermediate audit and verification results live in script variables. Each agent has its own context window; only the script's return value, the surviving findings, crosses into Claude's context.
answers.lifecycle: It runs when you invoke the saved command, type the ultracode keyword, or ask for a workflow in your own words, and it stops when the script returns, when you press `x` in /workflows, or at the runtime's cap of 1,000 agents per run. A stopped run is resumable only within the same session; exiting Claude Code makes the next session start it fresh.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on quality: the verification phase filters findings but nothing blocks a wrong verdict, and the runtime accepts no mid-run user input, so a shell command or MCP call outside your allowlist stalls the run behind a permission prompt. Stopping mid fan-out is expensive because replay follows start order and every agent that started after the first unfinished one reruns.
answers.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows require Claude Code v2.1.154 or later, are available on paid plans plus Anthropic API, Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry, and on Pro must be switched on in the Dynamic workflows row of /config. 400 files far exceeds the default `medium` size guideline (fewer than 15 agents, default since v2.1.219) and the 25-agent Large workflow warning added in v2.1.203, so raise workflowSizeGuideline; the symlink check that keeps the saved file where you chose needs v2.1.216.

answers.primary: An agent team. The session becomes the lead and spawns five teammates, each owning one hypothesis, with the spawn prompt instructing them to message each other and actively try to disprove the other theories. Consensus goes into a findings doc on disk, which is the durable artifact because teammate context windows never merge.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents. They report only back to the main agent and never talk to each other, so the adversarial cross-examination that makes a surviving hypothesis trustworthy cannot happen at all.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides who investigates what, when the debate has run its course, and what the consensus is; the harness supplies only the shared task list, the per-agent mailbox files under ~/.claude/teams/, and file locking on task claims. A TeammateIdle or TaskCompleted hook exiting with code 2 is the one harness-side lever that can force more work.
answers.context_boundary: Each teammate is a full independent Claude Code session with its own context window, loading CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills but not the lead's conversation history. What crosses is SendMessage traffic between teammates, shared task-list state, idle notifications to the lead, and whatever gets written to the findings doc.
answers.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate is spawned and each teammate runs until it goes idle, accepts a shutdown request, or the session ends. The team config directory is removed at session end; the task list under ~/.claude/tasks/ persists locally, governed by cleanupPeriodDays.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory throughout. Teammates can stop on errors instead of recovering, can fail to mark tasks complete and thereby block dependents, and the lead may declare the investigation finished early; Claude may also quietly spawn plain subagents instead of a team, and the agent panel alone does not tell you which happened.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default: set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment or nothing spawns. Documented behavior is as of v2.1.178, where TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist and cleanup is automatic; /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates, and five teammates cost roughly five independent context windows.

answers.primary: A subagent. Delegate "run the suite and report only the failing tests with their error messages" to a single subagent, and write it as a reusable test-runner definition in .claude/agents/ with tools limited to Bash, Read and Grep if you do this often. @-mention it so the delegation is guaranteed rather than left to Claude's judgment.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill. Skill instructions execute in the main conversation's context, so the tens of thousands of output lines would land in the very window you are trying to protect; a skill only solves this by setting context: fork, which is borrowing subagent isolation rather than being an alternative to it.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, but the harness owns the part that matters. Once the subagent runs, its tool output physically lives in a separate context window and only its final report returns. The model owns whether it delegates at all and what it chooses to put in that report.
answers.context_boundary: The subagent gets a fresh context window holding its system prompt, the delegation prompt Claude writes, your full CLAUDE.md hierarchy, and a git status snapshot. Only its final report crosses back, after the harness's subagent output scan; the raw suite output never leaves the subagent's window.
answers.lifecycle: It starts when Claude delegates and ends when the subagent returns its report. The transcript persists for the session under ~/.claude/projects/.../subagents/ and can be resumed with SendMessage; it is deleted after cleanupPeriodDays, 30 days by default.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on fidelity: nothing stops the subagent from summarizing badly, omitting failures, or truncating error text, and a run cut short by an API error returns partial output flagged as cut off. The real leak risk is that nothing prevents Claude from later rerunning the suite directly with Bash in your main conversation.
answers.version_caveat: As of v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default with a reduced built-in tool set, which still keeps Bash, Read, Grep and Glob, so this pattern is unaffected. Subagent output scanning requires v2.1.210 or later, and from v2.1.198 /agents no longer opens a creation wizard, so write the definition file yourself or ask Claude to write it.

answers.primary: An agent team of three teammates, one owning the frontend, one the backend API, one the test suite, coordinated by the lead through the shared task list while they message each other directly as the interface contract shifts. Select any teammate in the agent panel with the arrow keys and press Enter to open its transcript and type instructions straight into it.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents. They report only back to the main agent, so workers cannot keep each other informed as the contract evolves, and there is no equivalent of stepping into a peer as a first-class session and redirecting it without the orchestrator in the middle.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model, plus you. The lead partitions the work and assigns tasks turn by turn and you steer individual teammates directly; the harness only carries the mailbox, the task list with automatic dependency unblocking, and file locking on task claims.
answers.context_boundary: Three independent context windows, each loading project context (CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, skills) but none of the lead's history, so the contract has to be in the spawn prompt. Contract changes cross as SendMessage traffic and task-list updates; the code itself crosses through the shared working tree, since teammates are not worktree-isolated.
answers.lifecycle: The team exists from the first teammate spawn until each is shut down or the session ends, and each teammate's permission mode and model are fixed at spawn from the lead's settings. Tasks unblock automatically as their dependencies complete, and the team directory is cleaned up on session exit.
answers.failure_mode: The real hazard is file collisions: agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so the frontend/backend/tests partition is the only thing preventing overwrites and it is purely advisory. Task status can lag and block dependent work, and every teammate permission prompt surfaces in the lead session, so pre-approve common operations first.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and inert unless CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 is set. In-process mode is the default from v2.1.179 and works in any terminal; split panes require tmux or iTerm2 with the it2 CLI and are unsupported in the VS Code integrated terminal, Windows Terminal, and Ghostty. Teammates do not inherit the lead's /model unless you set Default teammate model in /config.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow. The check, fix and recheck loop plus the stop-after-two-rounds-without-progress rule live in the script's own JavaScript control flow, with an agent spawned per round to apply fixes, so the termination condition is executed code rather than a judgment call.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill. Skill instructions are followed by Claude in the main conversation, which means Claude rereads the loop condition and re-decides whether to continue on every round, which is exactly the babysitting and re-deciding the request rules out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the loop and evaluates the stopping condition; the model owns only what each fixing agent does inside a round.
answers.context_boundary: The script runs in the isolated workflow runtime; each round's type-check output and the diffs live in script variables and in that round's agent context window. Only the final result, whether the check passed and what changed, crosses into your conversation.
answers.lifecycle: It starts on the ultracode keyword, an explicit request for a workflow, or a saved command, and ends when the type check passes, when two consecutive rounds make no progress, at the 1,000-agent cap, or when you stop it from /workflows.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on termination, because the stopping rule is real code, but open on quality: workflow agents always run in acceptEdits and inherit your allowlist regardless of your session's permission mode, so fixes are auto-applied unreviewed, and the runtime takes no mid-run input, so your only intervention is stopping the run.
answers.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, with the Pro toggle in /config; /effort ultracode, which makes Claude reach for workflows unprompted, needs v2.1.203. A loop-shaped workflow is small so the default `medium` size guideline is not a constraint, but disableWorkflows in settings or managed settings, or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1, removes the mechanism entirely.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow that discovers the component files and then uses pipeline() to run one transform agent per file, each with isolation: worktree so it works in its own copy of the repository, followed by a verification step per file before that file counts as done.
answers.rejected_alternative: The bundled /batch skill. It is the packaged version of the same idea, worktree-isolated subagents that each open a pull request, but it targets 5 to 30 subagents, an order of magnitude below 500 files, and its orchestration is not a script you can reread, diff or rerun.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime executes the fan-out, bounds concurrency, and enforces worktree isolation: a Bash command whose working directory or git redirection resolves back to the main checkout fails outright, so "edits never collide" is mechanical rather than an instruction the model is asked to honor.
answers.context_boundary: Each file's transform runs in its own agent context window and its own git worktree, and results accumulate in script variables inside the isolated workflow runtime. Only the aggregate outcome crosses into your conversation, not 500 diffs.
answers.lifecycle: It runs from invocation to script return, with at most 16 agents concurrent and 1,000 agents per run. It is resumable within the session, but the replay rule means stopping mid fan-out reruns every agent that started after the first unfinished one, which on a 500-file run is most of them.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on correctness: the per-file verifier is another model judgment, so a subtly wrong transform can be marked verified, and a worktree is auto-cleaned only when its agent made no changes, so failed attempts leave debris. Cost is the other practical failure, since 500 agents is a large multiple of doing the same work in one session.
answers.version_caveat: Workflows need v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan. Worktree isolation tightened over several releases: v2.1.203 forced a subagent's Bash and PowerShell into its worktree, v2.1.210 extended the check to the whole repository, and v2.1.216 added the git-redirect command check, so on older builds an agent could still write into your main checkout. 500 files also exceeds every size guideline value, including `large` at fewer than 50 agents, so set `unrestricted` and expect the Large workflow warning.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: one reviewer agent per changed file via pipeline(), then a single synthesis agent that receives all 60 finding sets and returns one deduplicated, ranked summary.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Its distinguishing feature is teammates talking to each other, and the scenario states the reviewers have nothing to discuss, so you would pay the coordination overhead and one full context window per teammate for a capability you explicitly do not want.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The script guarantees one reviewer per file and that every finding set reaches the merge stage; the model owns the review quality inside each agent and the ranking judgment in the synthesis agent.
answers.context_boundary: Sixty reviewer context windows, each seeing only its own file, with the findings held in script variables inside the isolated workflow runtime. The only thing that reaches your conversation is the merged, ranked summary.
answers.lifecycle: One run per invocation, ending when the synthesis agent returns. If this should become the standing review for every branch, save the run's script from /workflows so it becomes a /command that reruns the identical orchestration.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at the merge: one synthesizer holding 60 finding sets is the bottleneck and can silently drop or over-merge real issues, and strictly per-file review misses defects that only appear across files. Sixty agents also trips the 25-agent Large workflow warning and runs 16 at a time, so it is slow rather than instant.
answers.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, with the Pro toggle in /config. The default `medium` size guideline aims for fewer than 15 agents and would push Claude to under-fan a 60-file review, so set `large` via /config or the workflowSizeGuideline settings key (guideline added v2.1.202; settings-file key and the medium default arrived in v2.1.219).

answers.primary: Three custom subagent definitions chained in the main conversation: a performance analyst, a fixer, and a verifier, each stored in .claude/agents/ so the roles are reusable, with Claude invoking them in order and folding each report into the next delegation prompt. Leave isolation unset so all three act on the same checkout.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team. The guidance points the other way for exactly this shape, sequential steps with heavy dependencies and same-file edits, where unisolated teammates overwrite each other and the coordination machinery buys nothing.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. Nothing in the harness enforces the order or the fidelity of the handoff; Claude decides when each stage is done and what of the previous report to carry forward. A SubagentStop hook in settings.json is the only harness-side gate you could bolt on.
answers.context_boundary: Each subagent gets a fresh context window containing only Claude's delegation prompt plus CLAUDE.md and git status, so the analyst's raw evidence does not carry over, only what Claude relays. Each stage's summary returns to the main conversation, which therefore holds the chain's connective tissue.
answers.lifecycle: Each subagent starts on delegation and ends when it returns its report; the chain ends when Claude judges all three stages done. Any stage can be continued with SendMessage instead of restarted, and all three count against the 200-subagent session limit and the 20-concurrent limit.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open twice over: the fixer may fix more or less than what was found because it works from a summary rather than the analyst's full evidence, and since v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default, so if Claude does not need a stage's result before continuing you can get overlapping edits on the same hot files.
answers.version_caveat: Background-by-default from v2.1.198 is the behavioral gate here; ask explicitly for foreground runs or set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 to keep the chain synchronous. Do not set isolation: worktree on these definitions, because each stage must see the previous stage's edits in the same checkout.

answers.primary: An agent team of three teammates, one on user experience, one on technical architecture, one playing devil's advocate, spawned with instructions to challenge each other's arguments as they form. Select any teammate in the agent panel and press Enter to open its transcript and redirect it mid-flight.
answers.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow that drafts the design from several angles. It can fan out three perspectives and weigh them against each other, but the runtime takes no mid-run user input and its agents do not converse, so both of your requirements, live cross-talk and jumping into one explorer, are lost.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model, with you in the loop. The lead spawns, assigns and synthesizes; the harness only carries messages and task state. Whether the three perspectives actually argue rather than merely report depends on the spawn prompt making the adversarial instruction explicit.
answers.context_boundary: Three independent context windows, each loading CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills but none of the lead's history, so the design brief must be in the spawn prompt. Arguments cross as direct teammate messages and task-list entries; your redirections cross when you type into a teammate's transcript.
answers.lifecycle: From the first teammate spawn until you shut the teammates down or end the session. While viewing a teammate, plain text and skills go to that teammate but built-in commands still run in the lead's session, and the teammate's model and fast mode are fixed at spawn time.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory. Claude may spawn plain subagents instead of a team and the agent panel will not distinguish them, teammates may report in parallel without ever engaging each other's arguments, and an idle teammate's row hides after 30 seconds so it looks stopped when it is only waiting for input.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and off by default: CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. The idle-row behavior described is v2.1.199 and later; /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates, so this exploration cannot be picked up in a later session; split-pane viewing needs tmux or iTerm2 with it2 and does not work in Windows Terminal or the VS Code integrated terminal.

answers.primary: Nested subagents. Delegate the review to one reviewer subagent that keeps Agent in its tools list, and have it dispatch a verifier subagent per finding from inside its own context, so only the reviewer's single final summary returns to you.
answers.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow. It would also keep the verification traffic out of your context, but it adds a version and plan gate, a launch approval prompt, and a whole script for a job that is 5 to 10 verifications deep and fits comfortably inside one delegated agent.
answers.enforcement_owner: Shared, and worth naming both halves: the harness enforces that a nested subagent's output stops at its parent and caps how deeply subagents nest, while the model owns whether the reviewer actually dispatches one verifier per finding and what survives into the summary.
answers.context_boundary: Three levels: your conversation, the reviewer's context window, and one context window per verifier. Verifier reports cross only into the reviewer's window; the single boundary your conversation sees is the reviewer's final summary, which passes through subagent output scanning on the way in.
answers.lifecycle: It starts when you delegate the review and ends when the reviewer returns its one summary. Every agent involved, reviewer and verifiers alike, counts against the 200-subagent session limit and the 20-concurrent limit, and 5 to 10 verifiers sit well under both.
answers.failure_mode: Fails silently open on the depth limit: when nesting is capped at one layer the harness simply withholds the Agent tool from the reviewer, which then verifies its own findings in a single context and still hands you one confident summary, so the loss of independent verification is invisible in the output you receive.
answers.version_caveat: The nesting default has moved repeatedly: v2.1.172 through v2.1.216 allowed five layers with no way to change it, v2.1.217 and v2.1.218 defaulted to one layer, which breaks this pattern outright, and v2.1.219 raised the default to three. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH (v2.1.217 or later) is how you set it, and the reviewer definition must not omit Agent from tools or list it in disallowedTools.
